• Height of Tree: To find the height of a node, we first need the heights of its left and right subtrees. Once both are known, the height is1 + max(leftHeight, rightHeight), making postorder traversal a natural fit. 
  • Size of Subtree:The size of a subtree depends on the sizes of both its left and right subtrees. After counting both sides, we add1for the current node itself.
  • Delete a Tree:When deleting a tree, child nodes must be deleted before their parent. Postorder traversal ensures children are processed first, making deletion safe.
  • Check Balanced Tree:To determine if a tree is balanced, each node needs the heights of its left and right subtrees. After receiving both heights, we check whether their difference is at most1.
  • Diameter of Tree:The diameter passing through a node depends on the heights of its left and right subtrees. Since both heights are needed before processing the current node, postorder traversal is commonly used.
  • Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA):Each subtree reports whether it contains one of the target nodes. When a node receives positive results from both left and right subtrees, that node becomes the Lowest Common Ancestor.
4. Classic Example: Height of Binary Tree

blocks.text: Left → Right → Root. Process children before parent the traversal you need when a node depends on its subtrees.
Postorder traversal visits the left subtree first, then the right subtree, and finally the current node the node is processed after (post) both its children.

The word "post" means the root comes last. This is the natural order for any computation where a parent node's result depends on values computed from its children first like calculating heights, sizes, or deleting a tree safely.

Key insight: Postorder is the "bottom-up" traversal. You always have complete information about a subtree before deciding what to do with its root. This makes it the go-to pattern for any "compute something about the tree" problem.

items: Step 1: Start at Node 1: Postorder follows the order Left → Right → Root, so we do not visit 1 immediately. First, we move to its left child 2.
Step 2: Move to Node 2: We still cannot visit 2 because both its left and right subtrees must be processed first. So we move to node 4.
Step 3: Visit Node 4: Node 4 is a leaf node with no children. Since both its left and right subtrees are already complete, we visit 4. Result: 4
Step 4: Visit Node 5: We return to node 2 and move to its right child 5. Since 5 is also a leaf node, we visit it immediately. Result: 4 → 5
Step 5: Visit Node 2: Both the left subtree (4) and right subtree (5) of node 2 have been processed. We can now visit 2. Result: 4 → 5 → 2
Step 6: Move to Node 3: We return to the root node 1. The left subtree is complete, so we move to the right child 3.
Step 7: Visit Node 6: Before visiting 3, postorder requires us to process its left subtree first. Node 6 is a leaf node, so we visit it. Result: 4 → 5 → 2 → 6
Step 8: Visit Node 7: Next, we move to the right child 7. Since it is also a leaf node, we visit it immediately. Result: 4 → 5 → 2 → 6 → 7
Step 9: Visit Node 3: Both children of 3 have now been processed, so we visit 3. Result: 4 → 5 → 2 → 6 → 7 → 3
Step 10: Visit Node 1: Finally, both the left subtree (2) and right subtree (3) of the root have been processed. We can now visit 1. Result: 4 → 5 → 2 → 6 → 7 → 3 → 1

blocks.text: Result:4 → 5 → 2 → 6 → 7 → 3 → 1. The root is always last. Every node waits until both its subtrees are fully proce
The key idea is that postorder always processes the left subtree first, then the right subtree, and visits the current node last. That's why the root node 1 is visited at the very end.
Implementation
Iterative Implementation
Iterative postorder is the trickiest of the three DFS traversals.
The cleanest approach: do a modified preorder (Root → Right → Left), collect in a list, then reverse it to get Left → Right → Root.
The reverse trick:

items: preorder is Root→Left→Right.
If you swap left/right pushes, you get Root→Right→Left.
Reverse that = Left→Right→Root = postorder.

blocks.text: Clean and easy to remember.
Postorder shines whenever a parent node's answer depends on answers from both children. You compute leaves first, bubble results upward, and the root gets the final combined answer.

blocks.text: This is the canonical postorder problem. Every node asks its children "what's your height?" before computing its own.
How it works:The function first calculates the height of the left subtree, then the height of the right subtree.
Once both heights are known, it computes the height of the current node as1 + max(leftHeight, rightHeight). Since the current node is processed after both children, this is a classic
Postorder Traversal (Left → Right → Root)pattern.

Notice: the three lines map exactly to postorder left call, right call, then use both results to compute the current node's value. This structure is the postorder template for almost every "compute a property" problem.

items: Time Complexity: The algorithm runs in O(n) time because every node in the tree is visited exactly once. At each node, only a constant amount of work is performed.

Space Complexity: The algorithm uses O(h) space, where h is the height of the tree. This space comes from the recursion stack. For a balanced tree, the height is O(log n), while for a completely skewed tree, the height becomes O(n)in the worst case.

In iterative version: forgetting to reverse you get Root→Right→Left without the reverse step.
Trying to do iterative postorder the "hard way" with a visited flag the reverse trick is cleaner.
Returning the wrong base case for height return -1 for null if counting edges, 0 if counting nodes.
In diameter/max path problems: confusing "return value" (used by parent) vs "global answer" (updated at each node).
Assuming postorder and preorder are reverses of each other they are NOT. Postorder is L→R→Root, reverse of preorder (Root→L→R) would be R→L→Root.
